articles.title: Mechanical/Inertial Collectors (Cyclones/Multiple Cyclones) Market To 2035: Cement and Mining Demand Supports Growth - News and Statistics - IndexBox
Chile Mulls Private-Sector Role in Codelco’s Mines and Infrastructure - Bloomberg.com

discussions.strategist:
Two headlines today, and one of them is noise.

The IndexBox item is a market-research release on mechanical cyclones through 2035. The headline gives no figures, base or forecast value. It's a sales pitch, not a signal, and I'm keeping it off the record.

The Bloomberg piece is the one that matters, but it isn't new. It's the Chile story we logged on 14 November from Mining.com. A second outlet helps, because two independent reports make "the government is considering it" more credible. It still isn't a decision. "Mulls" is the operative word. I'm working from the headline alone, so I won't add detail from a body I haven't read.

Where it fits. Codelco is the story the desk keeps circling: a 42,100-tonne overstatement with no stated period or basis, an Andina halt with no duration, and now a debate about private capital in its mines and infrastructure. Taken together, this is a governance and capital story, not a tonnage story. Dr Simon's framing holds. The reporting problem is a credibility discount. A private role could change how new capex is funded and who carries the cost of delay, but that plays out over years. It doesn't change 2026 tonnes.

Who gains and who loses? Private partners gain if the model gives them access. Codelco's board and the state give up some control. Investors lose if the production numbers can't be reconciled, and the overstatement is the reason that matters more than the policy debate.

Second-order risk: Chile's policy agenda is crowded. The BNamericas item on 2027 mining tax and fee changes sits in the same basket. If the government is reworking Codelco's ownership model and producer tax terms at once, the market will price that as jurisdiction risk rather than clean reform. (Historically, that kind of overlap tends to slow decisions rather than speed them.)

Watch for one thing: whether the government names specific assets in an official document. Vague "mulls" language is not a model.

PREDICTION: Chile's government publicly announces a formal decision, including a rejection, on a private-sector role in Codelco mines or infrastructure | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
discussions.geologist:
Colleagues, today's feed is thin. Two headlines came in. One is a market-research notice on cyclone separators, which tells us nothing about mine output or prices, so I'm setting it aside. The other is Bloomberg's report that Chile is weighing a private-sector role in Codelco's mines and infrastructure. That matters, but it is a story about governance and capital, not tonnes.

On Chile, Bloomberg is the second outlet to carry the "mulls" wording after Mining.com on 14 November. That's better than a single source, but it's still a government considering an option. No model, asset, stake or timetable has been named. Historically, when a state miner opens the door to private money, the first steps are often consultations and review panels, and the actual structure can take many months to settle. I would not read this as a decision.

Meldrum, you read Chile as a possible signal about future supply expectations over several years. I agree it could matter that way if private partners bring in capital for expansion. My concern is the sequence. Codelco is already carrying the 42,100-tonne "overstatement," with no period or basis stated. Until Codelco says what that figure is, the company's production numbers are a credibility discount, as Simon put it, and private participation debates will be read through that lens. Until the Codelco figure is reconciled, I'd keep Chile out of any copper supply conclusion.

The Capstone cut sits in the same bucket. We have no tonnes, asset or base year. Our first request should be for revised tonnes, the asset behind the restart slip, and the cause, all in one document. Until those arrive, the cut is a headline.

Guinea remains an enforcement story. At least 10 deaths are reported, all from one official source. My test is independent confirmation or an official count, and neither has arrived. I'm not treating this as lost supply.

Nothing new has come in on Barrick, Freeport, Centinela or Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, so their existing predictions and hold dates stand. The Barrick IPO is still "reported as filed" until we can read EDGAR.

On the LME 16 October settlement, the window closes 18 November, and nothing today changes that. We still have no copper price view for that date.

PREDICTION: Chile's government or Codelco publicly announces a formal decision, not a study or review, on private-sector participation in Codelco mines or infrastructure | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, your sequencing point sharpens my view. I called the Codelco overstatement a credibility discount, but you're right that it's a test. Until Codelco states the period and basis for the 42,100 tonnes, any private-capital debate will be read through that number. I accept that Chile stays out of any 2026 tonnes conclusion.

I still differ on one point. The capex funding question is the multi-year part. A private role could change who carries the cost of delay even if it leaves tonnes untouched. That's a 2028-and-beyond supply-expectations question, so I'd keep it on the list, flagged as slow.

Two things I missed. First, I treated Mining.com and Bloomberg as independent confirmation. Wire copy often shares an origin, so "two outlets" may be one government briefing. I'll check bylines before leaning on it again. Second, I said nothing about the Capstone cut. Your three asks (revised tonnes, the asset behind the restart slip, and the cause) are the right gate, and I'd adopt them as our standard.

On Guinea, your official-count test is the right one. Ten deaths from one source is a headline, not a supply event.

On predictions, I've merged our wording. The first now includes Codelco statements, since the company is likelier than the ministry to name assets first. The second keeps rejection as a valid outcome but excludes studies and reviews. Both stay at low confidence, because "mulls" comes with no timetable.

PREDICTION: Chile's government or Codelco publicly names at least one specific Codelco mine or infrastructure asset for private-sector participation, in an official government or company statement | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
PREDICTION: Chile's government or Codelco publicly announces a formal decision, including a rejection, on private-sector participation in Codelco mines or infrastructure (not a study or review) | BY: 2026-12-31 | CONFIDENCE: low
discussions.geologist_reply:
Meldrum, your point about the market reading Chile through the overstatement lens is the sharpest thing in the notes. Private partners will ask for reconciled production and reserve data before they price a stake, so the 42,100-tonne question will reach the deal table whether or not anyone plans for it.

Where I'd push back is on timing. I agree a private role could change how new capex is funded, but in my experience large porphyry expansions take years from approval to first ore, so the tonnes arrive well after any policy decision. Capital structure matters for the 2030s, not for next year's guidance.

I also see the infrastructure side differently. Smelters, ports, water and tailings are easier to carve out and name than an ore body, so if anything gets named first, it will probably be infrastructure. That would be a useful early signal, but it wouldn't tell us much about copper supply.

What I think we both missed is the Andina halt. Private money doesn't fix an operational stoppage, and nobody in the notes has said how long it lasts. Until it has a duration, it belongs in the same bucket as the overstatement.

On your first prediction, I'd keep the wider source wording, because a Codelco company statement naming an asset should count. Your version is narrower and easier to check, which is a fair trade. I'm also adding the rejection case to the second prediction, as you suggested.

discussions.summary:
Key stories:
- Bloomberg reports Chile is weighing a private-sector role in Codelco's mines and infrastructure. Mining.com carried the same "mulls" framing on 14 November, but no model, asset, stake, or timetable has been named.
- Codelco's 42,100-tonne overstatement has no stated period or basis, and the Andina halt has no duration. Both are treated as credibility tests.
- The Capstone production cut lacks tonnes, asset, and base year.
- Guinea reports at least 10 deaths from one official source, which the notes treat as an enforcement story rather than lost supply.
- The IndexBox cyclone-separator notice is set aside as noise.

Where they agree:
- Chile is a governance and capital story, not a 2026 tonnage story.
- Codelco must reconcile the overstatement before its production figures are trusted, and no copper supply conclusion should rest on Chile yet.
- The Capstone cut needs revised tonnes, the asset, and the cause before it counts.

Where they disagree:
- Meldrum sees a private role as a possible 2028-plus supply-expectations question, because it could change who carries the cost of delay. Yukon agrees capital structure matters, but argues it bears on the 2030s and says it tells little about copper supply.
- Meldrum would count a Codelco statement naming an asset. Yukon would require a government statement for the formal decision prediction, and he expects infrastructure to be named first.
